lessons.title: Observability Mental Model
lessons.summary: Observability Mental Model Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow Monitoring asks known questions such as “is error rate above 5%?” Observability is broader: it lets engineers investigate unfamiliar failures by correlating multiple signals. TaskFlow uses logs for discrete events, metrics for aggregate trends, traces…
lessons.body:
Observability Mental Model

Monitoring asks known questions such as “is error rate above 5%?” Observability is broader: it lets
engineers investigate unfamiliar failures by correlating multiple signals. TaskFlow uses logs for
discrete events, metrics for aggregate trends, traces for request paths, and error monitoring for
grouped exceptions with release context.

METRICS: how often/how        TRACES: where time              ERRORS: which failures
LOGS: what happened
much                          flowed                          need action
→                                →                              →

Figure 2. Four complementary signals

Questions each signal answers
Signal                                                            Best questions

Logs                                                              What happened on request 7fd2? Which business decision
failed?

Metrics                                                           What is p95 latency? Is 5xx rate rising? How many requests
are active?

Traces                                                            Which dependency/span consumed 1.8 seconds?

Error monitoring                                                  Which exception regressed after release X? How many
users/requests were affected?

No signal replaces the others. A metric may show a latency spike but not the exact failing request. A
log may explain one request but not reveal whether the problem affects 1% or 80% of traffic.
Production caution: Do not turn user IDs, task IDs, raw URLs, emails, or arbitrary search text into
metric labels. High-cardinality attributes can create unbounded time-series growth and cost.

lessons.title: Structured Logging Log Levels and Events
lessons.summary: Structured Logging, Levels, and Events Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow NestJS 12 can emit JSON directly through ConsoleLogger and treats plain objects passed after the message as structured metadata. TaskFlow keeps that built-in path instead of adding another logging library before a concrete…
lessons.body:
Structured Logging, Levels, and Events

NestJS 12 can emit JSON directly through ConsoleLogger and treats plain objects passed after the
message as structured metadata. TaskFlow keeps that built-in path instead of adding another logging
library before a concrete need appears.
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, {
logger: new ConsoleLogger({
json: process.env.NODE_ENV === 'production',
}),
});

private readonly logger = new Logger(TasksService.name);

this.logger.log('Task status updated', {
requestId, taskId, fromStatus, toStatus, userId,
});

Stable event fields
Field                                                     Meaning

requestId                                                 Correlates one incoming HTTP request and downstream
work

event                                                     Stable machine-searchable event name

context                                                   Service/module emitting the record

userId                                                    Internal domain ID when policy permits

workspaceId                                               Tenant scope when relevant

durationMs                                                Measured operation duration

errorCode                                                 Application error code, not raw secret-bearing exception
text

Log level policy
• debug: local diagnosis and temporary high-detail context; normally disabled or sampled in
production.

• log/info: expected lifecycle or meaningful business/operational events.

• warn: degraded/recoverable state that deserves attention but did not fail the request.

• error: request/job failed or invariant unexpectedly broke.

• fatal: process cannot continue safely.
Production caution: Never log bearer tokens, refresh tokens, cookies, service-role keys,
DATABASE_URL, passwords, signed upload tokens, or full request bodies by default.

lessons.title: Correlation IDs and Request Context
lessons.summary: Correlation IDs and Request Context Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow TaskFlow already uses Fastify request.id. Phase 30 formalizes it as correlation context and returns x-request-id to clients. The same identifier belongs in logs and error-monitoring metadata so a support ticket can move directly…
lessons.body:
Correlation IDs and Request Context

TaskFlow already uses Fastify request.id. Phase 30 formalizes it as correlation context and returns
x-request-id to clients. The same identifier belongs in logs and error-monitoring metadata so a support
ticket can move directly from a user-visible request ID to internal evidence.

x-request-id /                                              downstream
Sentry                              response
Browser                Fastify              Nest logs                              API/storage
tag/context                         x-request-id
request.id                                                  events
→                     →                    →                 →                 →

Figure 3. Correlation flow

const requestId = request.id;
reply.header('x-request-id', requestId);

logger.log('Request completed', {
requestId,
method: request.method,
route: request.routeOptions?.url ?? request.url,
statusCode: reply.statusCode,
durationMs,
});

Use normalized route templates where possible. Logging `/tasks/8c1...` as a route dimension is less
useful than `/tasks/:id` and creates cardinality/noise.
Key idea: Correlation ID is not authentication and should not carry secrets. It is only a join key across
telemetry.

lessons.title: Traces and OpenTelemetry Concepts
lessons.summary: Traces and OpenTelemetry Concepts Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow A trace models one operation as related spans. For TaskFlow, an HTTP request may contain spans for authorization, repository/database work, Storage signing, or an external API. This makes “the request took 1.9s” actionable by…
lessons.body:
Traces and OpenTelemetry Concepts

A trace models one operation as related spans. For TaskFlow, an HTTP request may contain spans for
authorization, repository/database work, Storage signing, or an external API. This makes “the request
took 1.9s” actionable by showing which part consumed the time.

HTTP PATCH
TasksService                Prisma UPDATE
/tasks/:id                  Auth [15ms]                                                              serialize [8ms]
[1850ms]                    [1810ms]
[1900ms]
→                       →                             →                   →

Figure 5. Trace example

OpenTelemetry provides vendor-neutral APIs and conventions for traces, metrics, logs, and context
propagation. TaskFlow uses the concepts and @opentelemetry/api 1.9.1 as the stable API line, but
does not hard-lock the Node SDK in this phase because the current `@opentelemetry/sdk-node`
package is explicitly marked experimental.

Instrumentation rule
• Prefer automatic instrumentation for generic HTTP/runtime behavior.

• Add custom spans only around operations whose latency or failure meaning matters to TaskFlow.

• Use semantic/stable span names, not raw user input.

• Do not create one span for every trivial function call.
Key idea: Observability code should illuminate architecture, not become a second architecture that
dominates business code.

lessons.title: Database Realtime Storage and Background Work Observability
lessons.summary: Database, Realtime, Storage, and Background Work Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow Request logs alone are not enough once TaskFlow performs database, Realtime, Storage, and later worker/background operations. Each boundary needs useful events and durations without copying sensitive payloads. Boundary Useful evidence Prisma/PostgreSQL operation/query…
lessons.body:
Database, Realtime, Storage, and
Background Work

Request logs alone are not enough once TaskFlow performs database, Realtime, Storage, and later
worker/background operations. Each boundary needs useful events and durations without copying
sensitive payloads.

Boundary                                           Useful evidence

Prisma/PostgreSQL                                  operation/query class, duration, failure category,
transaction outcome; never SQL with secrets/PII by default

Realtime                                           channel/topic category, subscribe/reconnect result,
duration, failure reason category

Storage                                            attachmentId, operation type, size bucket, duration, Storage
error category; never signed token

Background jobs                                    job type/id, attempt, queued/start/end timestamps,
outcome, retry category

For slow database work, start with endpoint/operation latency and repository-level timing. Add
query-plan investigation only after evidence points at a database bottleneck. Logging every SQL
statement in production can create cost, noise, and privacy risk.
Production caution: Do not use high-cardinality business object IDs as metric dimensions. IDs belong in
logs/traces where individual-event context is appropriate.

lessons.body:
Dashboards, SLOs, and Alert Design

A dashboard should answer an operational question. A good first TaskFlow dashboard focuses on
traffic, errors, latency, and saturation/health rather than decorative charts.

Panel                                                  Question

Request rate                                           Is traffic normal?

5xx / error-code rate                                  Are users failing?

p50 / p95 / p99 latency                                How slow is the experience, including tail latency?

Readiness / instance count                             Can healthy replicas serve traffic?

DB/connection/runtime saturation                       Is a constrained resource causing the symptom?

Release marker                                         Did behavior change after a deploy?

Alert on symptoms first
• High user-visible error rate for a sustained window.

• p95 latency over a meaningful threshold for a sustained window.

• No ready instances / repeated readiness failure.

• Critical background workflow repeatedly failing.

• Security/abuse alerts with clear actionability.
Production caution: Avoid alerts like “one exception occurred” or “CPU hit 71% once.” Alerts that
constantly fire without requiring action train engineers to ignore them.

lessons.summary: Privacy, Redaction, and Telemetry Cost Full Stack Developer 2026 Complete - TaskFlow Telemetry is a data system. Treat it with the same care as application data. Every log field, trace attribute, event breadcrumb, and metric label has privacy, security, retention, and cost implications. TaskFlow redaction…
lessons.body:
Privacy, Redaction, and Telemetry Cost

Telemetry is a data system. Treat it with the same care as application data. Every log field, trace
attribute, event breadcrumb, and metric label has privacy, security, retention, and cost implications.

TaskFlow redaction baseline
Never record                                          Safer alternative

Authorization / Cookie headers                        requestId, auth failure category

Access/refresh tokens                                 token-valid/expired/wrong-issuer category

DATABASE_URL/service key                              dependency name + sanitized error category

Full form/request body                                specific allowlisted metadata

Uploaded file contents                                attachmentId, MIME, size bucket

Password/MFA/reset token                              event outcome only

Sampling can reduce high-volume trace cost. Logging should also avoid repeating the same verbose
context at every layer. Keep enough detail to diagnose failures while controlling retention and vendor
spend.
Key idea: If a field is not required to answer an operational question, do not collect it “just in case.”

Incident Debugging, Runbooks, and Testing

Observability becomes valuable during an incident only if engineers know how to use it. Phase 30 adds
a small runbook structure that moves from symptom to correlated evidence instead of random code
changes.

identif                                        correl

inspec        pick re                         isolate                    verify
ted ro                                         s/trace                      mitiga                    pectiv
Alert                          t metri       quest/                          depen                      recove

cs            error                           dency                      ry

→              →              →                →              →             →            →            →

Figure 6. Incident path

Failure drill: slow Task updates
• Confirm p95/p99 increase and the affected route.

• Check whether the issue began after a release.

• Open a slow trace/request and identify the longest span.

• If Prisma/PostgreSQL dominates, inspect repository query behavior and database evidence.

• If Storage/Realtime dominates, inspect that boundary instead.

• Mitigate first, then optimize with evidence.

Automated checks
• Every response has x-request-id.

• Structured request completion logs include normalized route/status/duration.

• Secrets are absent from captured logs/errors.

• /health/live stays up during a recoverable dependency issue.

• /health/ready fails when PostgreSQL is intentionally unavailable.

• Synthetic exception reaches the non-production Sentry project.

• Alert rules are test-fired before production reliance.

Hands-On Lab and Phase Exit

Level 1 - Follow
• Enable JSON logging in production mode.

• Add a request completion interceptor/middleware with requestId, route, status, and duration.

• Expose liveness and readiness endpoints.

Level 2 - Integrate
• Install/configure @nestjs/terminus 12.0.0 and wire PostgreSQL readiness.

• Add @sentry/nestjs 10.75.0 and @sentry/nextjs 10.75.0 in non-production first.

• Propagate requestId into error monitoring.

Level 3 - Observe
• Create request-rate, error-rate, and latency views.

• Record a deliberate 500 and trace it from response requestId to logs/error monitor.

• Simulate PostgreSQL outage and verify liveness versus readiness behavior.

Level 4 - Engineer
Design an observability plan for a payroll finalization workflow. Identify the logs, metrics, trace spans,
health dependencies, alert condition, and sensitive data that must never be recorded.

Phase exit criteria
• A production request can be correlated across public error response, logs, and error monitoring.

• TaskFlow has explicit liveness and readiness semantics.

• Latency is measured as a distribution, not only an average.

• Metrics avoid high-cardinality labels.

• Telemetry has a written redaction/privacy policy.

• Dashboards and alerts answer operational questions and have owners/runbooks.
Key idea: Phase 30 is complete when an engineer can diagnose a realistic failure from emitted
evidence without adding emergency console.log statements.

lessons.body:
Guided Build Lab — Phase 30: Logging & Observability

Purpose
Make production behavior observable with structured logs, request correlation, error monitoring, metrics, traces/signals, and actionable alerts.

Deliverable
Observability layer connecting Next.js/API errors and request IDs to structured logs and monitoring releases.

Before you touch the code
Open the previous phase checkpoint, run the repository's verification commands, and make sure Git is clean. A guided lab is useful only when you know which change introduced a failure. Write down the current browser/API/database behavior you expect before modifying anything.

Architecture trace
request/user action -> correlation ID -> structured events -> error monitor/metrics -> dashboard/alert -> diagnosis

Read this flow left to right, then right to left. For each arrow, say what data crosses the boundary, which side trusts the other, and what evidence would prove that this boundary works. This habit prevents framework APIs from becoming disconnected memorization.

Step 1 — Define the minimum structured fields every API request/error log should carry.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 2 — Generate or propagate a request ID and return it so support can correlate client reports.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 3 — Redact secrets and PII deliberately before adding rich context.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 4 — Integrate error monitoring for both Next.js and NestJS and tag releases by commit SHA.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 5 — Add a few meaningful application/HTTP/database signals rather than hundreds of vanity metrics.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Step 6 — Simulate a production-style error and walk from user-visible request ID to logs/monitoring evidence.
Do the smallest version of this step first. After the change, stop and verify it before continuing. Use terminal output, HTTP responses, browser DevTools, tests, or database inspection depending on the boundary. If the result differs from your prediction, do not add more code; explain the mismatch and fix the earliest failing assumption.

Checkpoint
When the lab works, inspect git diff. Remove accidental debugging output and unrelated edits. Run type checking/tests/build commands relevant to this phase. Commit the checkpoint with a message that describes the capability added, not merely the files changed.

Explain-back
Without looking at the lesson, explain why each layer in the architecture trace exists, what this phase added to TaskFlow, and what would break if the new responsibility were moved to the wrong layer. If you cannot explain the boundary, repeat the trace before moving on.

lessons.title: Debugging Workshop
lessons.summary:
Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.
lessons.body:
Debugging Workshop — Phase 30: Logging & Observability

Goal
Learn to diagnose this phase's failures systematically instead of reinstalling packages, changing random configuration, or copying a fix without understanding it.

The debugging loop
1. Reproduce the failure with the smallest reliable action.
2. Capture the exact symptom: command, status code, stack trace, network request, database state, or UI state.
3. Locate the earliest boundary where actual behavior diverges from expected behavior.
4. Form one hypothesis.
5. Change one variable.
6. Re-run the same reproduction.
7. Keep the fix only if the evidence supports the hypothesis.

Boundary walk
request/user action -> correlation ID -> structured events -> error monitor/metrics -> dashboard/alert -> diagnosis

Start at the visible symptom and walk backward. Do not debug the database when the browser never sent the request. Do not debug React state when the API is returning a deterministic 403. The boundary walk tells you which evidence to collect next.

Failure drill 1 — console.log strings with no searchable structure
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 2 — Tokens/passwords in logs
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 3 — Alerts on every exception rather than user-impacting symptoms
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Failure drill 4 — No release/environment tags so errors cannot be tied to deployments
Create or imagine this failure in a safe development environment. Write the expected symptom first. Then list the two or three observations that would distinguish this failure from neighboring causes. Repair it with the smallest change and verify the original reproduction no longer fails.

Do not hide the evidence
Avoid immediately clearing caches, deleting lockfiles, resetting the database, disabling security checks, or reinstalling everything. Those actions may erase the evidence that teaches you what was wrong. Use them only after you can explain why they are relevant.

Debugging exit ticket
Pick one failure from this workshop and write a short incident note: symptom, scope, root cause, fix, verification, and prevention. This is the same communication pattern used in professional bug reports and production incident follow-ups.

Phase Synthesis & Independent Challenge — Logging & Observability

Mission
Rebuild the capability of Phase 30 without following the exact code line-by-line. The goal is transfer: can you use the ideas when the variable names, UI, or route shape changes?

Required outcome
Make production behavior observable with structured logs, request correlation, error monitoring, metrics, traces/signals, and actionable alerts.

Required artifact
Observability layer connecting Next.js/API errors and request IDs to structured logs and monitoring releases.

Constraints
• Start from the previous phase checkpoint or a fresh branch.
• Use the course architecture boundaries, but do not copy the reference implementation until after your first attempt.
• Keep changes scoped to the capability.
• Preserve validation, authorization, error handling, and observability expectations already earned in earlier phases.
• Record any design decision where more than one implementation is reasonable.

Acceptance criteria
• Can correlate one request across layers.
• Can log useful context safely.
• Can distinguish logs/metrics/traces/error monitoring.
• Can define an actionable alert.

Independent build sequence
1. Define the minimum structured fields every API request/error log should carry.
2. Generate or propagate a request ID and return it so support can correlate client reports.
3. Redact secrets and PII deliberately before adding rich context.
4. Integrate error monitoring for both Next.js and NestJS and tag releases by commit SHA.
5. Add a few meaningful application/HTTP/database signals rather than hundreds of vanity metrics.
6. Simulate a production-style error and walk from user-visible request ID to logs/monitoring evidence.

Self-review
Compare your implementation to the reference only after the acceptance criteria pass. Differences are not automatically mistakes. For each difference, ask: does it preserve the same contract, security boundary, correctness, maintainability, and operational behavior? Keep the alternative when you can justify it with evidence.

Stretch challenge
Change one assumption: more users, a second tenant, a slow network, an expired session, a concurrent mutation, a deployment restart, or a failed dependency. Predict whether your design still behaves correctly. If not, document the next architectural improvement rather than adding complexity blindly.

Phase exit
Run the relevant checks, inspect Git diff, and write a three-sentence summary: what the system can do now, which boundary owns the new responsibility, and which failure you now know how to diagnose. Only then mark the phase complete.

lessons.body:
Mastery Capstone Lab

This is the transfer exercise for Phase 30: Logging & Observability. The detailed lessons are now closed-book reference material. Your task is to prove that the phase outcome can be reproduced from requirements, repository evidence, and debugging—not by copying a finished implementation.

Target artifact
Observability layer connecting Next.js/API errors and request IDs to structured logs and monitoring releases.

Acceptance criteria
- Write the behavior and constraints before implementation.
- Identify the owning layer and every boundary crossed.
- Implement the smallest complete vertical slice.
- Verify the happy path from outside the implementation.
- Demonstrate at least one expected failure path.
- Run the phase-relevant quality checks.
- Review the diff for accidental duplication, leaked responsibilities, missing validation/authorization, and hidden environment assumptions.

Evidence packet
Save the command/request used, expected result, actual result, one failure reproduction, the fix, and a short explanation of why the final responsibility belongs where it does. This packet is more valuable than a screenshot of a green page because it demonstrates repeatable engineering reasoning.

Stretch
Change one requirement after the first implementation. Measure which files must change. If a tiny domain change causes unrelated layers to move, use that evidence to discuss coupling before adding another abstraction.

objectives: Make production behavior observable with structured logs, request correlation, error monitoring, metrics, traces/signals, and actionable alerts.
Produce a reproducible evidence packet for success and failure.
Defend the architecture and identify one improvement without overengineering.
workshop.why: A guided lesson proves you can follow. A capstone proves you can transfer the model to a requirement with fewer cues.

Generate or propagate a request ID and return it so support can correlate client reports.
Redact secrets and PII deliberately before adding rich context.
Integrate error monitoring for both Next.js and NestJS and tag releases by commit SHA.
Add a few meaningful application/HTTP/database signals rather than hundreds of vanity metrics.
Simulate a production-style error and walk from user-visible request ID to logs/monitoring evidence.
Run the phase mastery checklist without looking at the provided implementation.
Perform a short architecture review and document one trade-off you consciously accepted.

references.preview:
# TaskFlow incident runbook
1. Confirm symptom, start time, affected route/workflow, environment, release.
2. Inspect request/error rate and p95/p99 latency.
3. Select a representative request/error and correlate by requestId.
4. Use traces/logs to isolate the slow/failing boundary.
5. Mitigate first; verify recovery with metrics and health checks.
6. Create follow-up action for root cause, missing telemetry, and test coverage.

# Observability field catalog

Allowed common fields: requestId, event, context, method, normalizedRoute, statusCode, durationMs, environment, release, workspaceId (logs/traces only where needed), internal userId (policy-dependent).

Never record: Authorization headers, cookies, access/refresh tokens, passwords, service-role keys, DATABASE_URL, signed upload tokens, raw uploaded content.

Metric labels should remain low-cardinality: method, normalized route, status class, environment.

# TaskFlow Phase 30 observability snapshot
Study snapshot only. Merge into the evolving TaskFlow repository intentionally. Do not copy secrets into examples. The design keeps NestJS structured logging, Terminus health checks, Sentry error/performance monitoring, and vendor-neutral OpenTelemetry concepts separated by responsibility.

# Phase 30 version lock
- @nestjs/terminus 12.0.0
- @sentry/nestjs 10.75.0
- @sentry/nextjs 10.75.0
- @opentelemetry/api 1.9.1
- @opentelemetry/sdk-node 0.222.0 is discussed but not hard-locked as a production dependency because the package describes itself as experimental.

# Observability verification matrix
- x-request-id returned on API responses.
- request completion log contains requestId, normalized route, status, duration.
- logs contain no Authorization/Cookie/secret values.
- /health/live remains 200 while process is healthy.
- /health/ready fails when test PostgreSQL is unavailable.
- synthetic error appears in non-production Sentry with requestId.
- p95/p99 latency can be derived from histogram/distribution telemetry.
- metrics contain no userId/taskId/requestId labels.
- alert test reaches the intended channel and points to a runbook.
